ch09.note: The Executive Yuan (行政院), the cabinet or administrative branch of the Republic of China's government, the highest organ of ordinary civil administration under the president.

ch09.anchor: struck dumb as cicadas in the cold
ch09.note: The idiom jin ruo han chan (噤若寒蝉), 'silent as a cicada in the cold'—cicadas fall mute once the weather turns—for someone who keeps his mouth shut out of fear and dares not speak.

Niu gui she shen (牛鬼蛇神), 'ox-headed demons and snake-bodied spirits,' a Buddhist image for a rabble of monsters, hence any assortment of bad characters. The Communists made it a stock label of denunciation, notorious in the Cultural Revolution for the class enemies it condemned.

ch09.anchor: sworn brother in life and death
ch09.note: Unrelated men could bind themselves as sworn brothers (拜把子 / 结义) in a formal oath before Heaven, pledging mutual loyalty 'in life and death.' The tie carried obligations as strong as blood kinship and runs all through this world of soldiers and secret men.

'The great smoke' (大烟) is opium; to be 'on the great smoke' is to be an opium addict. The drug, forced on China through the nineteenth-century Opium Wars and endemic well into the twentieth century, is a recurring mark of dissipation in these pages.
Japanese materiel was dated by the reigning emperor's era. The Taishō era ran 1912–1926, so 'Taishō 15' is 1926. (The following Shōwa era, mentioned elsewhere, began in 1926.)

The Type 38 rifle (三八式, the 'Arisaka'), the standard bolt-action infantry rifle of the Imperial Japanese Army, adopted in 1905 (the 38th year of Meiji) and carried by Japanese troops throughout the war in China.

A 'Special Service Agency' (特務機関, tokumu kikan) was a field intelligence and covert-operations office of the Japanese army. The one at Fengtian (Mukden, today Shenyang) ran subversion, bribery, and puppet-building across Manchuria and North China; the 'Ume Kikan' met later in the book was another such agency.

ch09.anchor: using the barbarian to curb the barbarian
ch09.note: Yi yi zhi yi (以夷制夷), 'use the barbarian to control the barbarian'—an old maxim of Chinese frontier statecraft, setting one outside power against another so they wear each other down rather than turn on China.

The 'united front' (统一战线) was the Communists' strategy of allying, for a time, with other parties and classes against a common enemy—twice, in the 1920s and again from 1937, with the Nationalists themselves. Chen uses the term with contempt, as a tactic of infiltration to be abandoned once its purpose was served.

Chinese festivals and much daily reckoning followed the lunar calendar, whose months are counted as 'moons.' The twelfth moon is the last month of the lunar year, the depth of winter just before the New Year; the Lantern Festival that closes the New Year falls on the fifteenth of the first moon.

A hutong (胡同) is one of the narrow residential lanes, formed by the walls of courtyard houses, that make up the old fabric of Beijing; the city's addresses and neighborhoods are largely named by them.

'Face' (面子, mianzi) is one's standing, dignity, and reputation in the eyes of others—something to be given, saved, or lost. The regard for it governs much of the caution, courtesy, and maneuvering in this book, and here shapes how Dai Li must be handled.

The 29th Army (二十九军), Song Zheyuan's force garrisoning the Beiping–Tianjin region in the mid-1930s. Its troops fought the opening clash of the full war at the Marco Polo Bridge in July 1937 and are remembered for the big-sword companies that fought the Japanese at the Great Wall passes.
